newsitem.title: UK: Horse racing-Irish eyes smiling again at Cheltenham.
newsitem.headline: Horse racing-Irish eyes smiling again at Cheltenham.

text.p: Irish eyes were smiling again on Wednesday as Ireland celebrated two victories at the Cheltenham Festival of Racing after they had drawn a disappointing blank on the previous day.

"Up Ireland. Now roll on the Gold Cup," one Irishman shouted from the stands as he watched Willie Mullins-trained 6-1 chance Florida Pearl win the last of seven races run at the Prestbury Park racecourse on Wednesday.

Three Irish-trained horses head the betting for Thursday's Gold Cup with 1996 champion Imperial Call the ante-post favourite at 5-1. Dorans Pride and Danoli are both quoted at 6-1 for the feature presentation.
Ten thousand Irish punters will attend Cheltenham on Thursday, hoping that Ireland's winning streak will continue.
What a difference a day makes in racing.

Irish punters were in despair in the public houses of Cheltenham on Tuesday evening as they grappled to come to terms with the fact that not one horse trained in Ireland had succeeded in winning on the first day of the Festival.
"If Istabraq does not win tomorrow I will have to try and cash a cheque with a bookmaker. I have hardly any cash left," Michael Hickey from County Mayo said.
A look at the betting for the Sun Alliance Novice Hurdle, the first race run on Wednesday, would seem to indicate that Hickey was not alone.

Istabraq's official starting price for the Novices' Hurdle, with 20 runners in the field, was 6-5 favourite. He had been generally available at 6-4 in the bookmaker shops at Cheltenham on Wednesday morning.

"I backed him and got my losses of yesterday back. I had a few quid on Finnegan's Hollow yesterday but downed tools after his fall but I chased my losses with this horse and now show a small profit," Istabraq's owner John Paul McManus said.
So too, it would appear, do many other Irish punters after Ireland's welcome Wednesday double.
As darkness descended over Cheltenham racecourse, many of the 10,000 Irish punters who had attended on the penultimate day of the Festival were still crowded into the bars.
The stout flowed freely, the singing had started and all the talk was of the possibility of a horse trained in Ireland winning the 1997 Gold Cup.
